title: What is Gradient Descent?
description: How gradient descent minimizes the loss function, how stochastic and batch updates differ, and why gradients vanish or explode.
content:
**Gradient descent** is an optimization algorithm used to minimize the **loss function** by iteratively adjusting the parameters of the model in the direction of the steepest descent of the loss function gradient. This process continues until the algorithm converges to a minimum point of the loss function, which indicates optimal parameters.

The **learning rate** determines the size of the steps taken after each iteration of the gradient descent algorithm:
• Too small a learning rate may lead to slow convergence.
• Too large a learning rate may lead to oscillating around the loss function minimum.

Therefore, it is essential to choose the learning rate either efficiently or dynamically.

Variations of gradient descent differ in how much data is used for one parameter update:
• Batch gradient descent - updates the model parameters after iterating through the entire dataset.
• Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) - updates the model parameters after one record or a very small amount of records (a mini-batch) chosen randomly from the dataset.

The random selection helps SGD converge faster and be computationally more efficient, though SGD may exhibit more noise in the parameter updates compared to batch gradient descent. Generally, SGD works better, especially in high-dimensional problems.

During **backpropagation**, gradients that are propagated back through many layers can cause two well-known problems:
• Vanishing gradients
• Exploding gradients

**Vanishing gradients** occur when gradients become exceedingly small as they are propagated back through many layers. This means that the weights in the earlier layers receive minimal updates and therefore learn very slowly or not at all. To mitigate this problem it is useful to:
• Use Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activations or their variants
• Be careful about weight initialization techniques
• Incorporate architecture adjustments like residual connections

**Exploding gradients** are the opposite problem: gradients become excessively large during backpropagation, which can cause the weights to update to enormous values and lead to numerical instability. To handle this problem it is useful to:
• Implement gradient clipping
• Be careful about weight initialization
• Use layer or batch normalization techniques
